newsitem.title: USA: Investigators begin second phase of King murder weapon probe.
newsitem.headline: Investigators begin second phase of King murder weapon probe.

text.p: A team of firearms investigators on Wednesday began using a high-power electron microscope to analyse bullet fragments taken from the body of slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr.

The microscope work at CamScan USA in Cranberry Township, Pennsylvania, is the second phase of a probe that began last week at a University of Rhode Island crime lab, where investigators test fired the Remington rifle linked to King's 1968 assasination at a Memphis, Tennessee, hotel.
James Earl Ray, 69, confessed to the murder in 1969 but later recanted his story. His fingerprints were found on the rifle but it was never proven to be the murder weapon.
The microscope test may prove whether the bullet that killed King was fired from the rifle.
Ray's attorney, William Pepper, said the test results could win him a new trial, although Ray is terminally ill with liver disease.

"If there's a match (between the bullet and the rifle) we're going to have to regard that weapon as the actual murder weapon," Pepper told reporters at a news conference. "But it doesn't change the historical position that has been taken by the defence in this case that James Earl Ray turned the rifle over (to someone else) the evening prior to the murder and he never saw it again."

Robert Hathaway, a University of Rhode Island criminalist and the team's lead investigator, said the tests could be inconclusive but he was optimistic that the rifle will either be proven or excluded as the murder weapon.
"We're optimistic on the testings that we did last week that perhaps we can find some conclusion here one way or another. That's not to say that we couldn't come up inconclusive also," he said.
Pepper said the test results will be turned over to court authorities in Tennessee before being released publicly.
Under Tennessee law, a closed case can be re-opened if there is a reasonable possibility that technology that did not exist at the time of a crime could prove a person's innocence.
